RagShortTexts: Christians pray for the dead and tend graves; kin meetings involve food and alms.
Clergy and families can differ over conduct at graves, while poor homes balance subsistence.

Variants.Content:
Rus Christians remember the dead in worship and visit family graves to pray, tend the surroundings and meet relatives. Remembering names and seeking clerical prayers depend on kin ties and daily devotion. Graves also need accessible paths, boundaries and repairs to damaged woodwork.

Kin share food, receive visitors or give to the poor, using the living household’s grain, drink and time. Families may see an act as respect for ancestors while clergy oppose food or drink intended to sustain spirits. Debt, orphan care and work arrangements continue after bereavement and return to discussion at grave visits.
Noble memorial gifts concern heirs and dependants as well as devotion. Public alms do not replace continuing support for the dead person’s household.
Soldiers may entrust death news and belongings to companions. Kin need names and a clear account; grave visits require routes, leave and travel provisions.
Poor families count grain for visitors and value meals from neighbours. Children and elders need ongoing support beyond a single memorial gathering.
